title: Two workshop technologies
prompt: Harbor needs 2 labor hours per bicycle and 6 per table. Valley needs 4 hours per bicycle and 8 per table. With labor as the only input, which specialization follows comparative advantage?
correct: Harbor in bicycles; Valley in tables.
wrong: Harbor in tables; Valley in bicycles.
Harbor in both because it uses fewer hours in both.
Valley in bicycles because its bicycle productivity is relatively low.
explanation: A bicycle costs 1/3 table in Harbor and 1/2 table in Valley. Harbor has the lower bicycle opportunity cost; Valley has the lower table opportunity cost.

title: A mutually beneficial exchange rate
prompt: A country sacrifices 2 sacks of grain for one bolt of cloth; its partner sacrifices 5. With constant opportunity costs and no trade costs, which price gives both a strict production-based gain from exchanging cloth for grain?
correct: 3 sacks of grain per bolt of cloth.
wrong: 1 sack of grain per bolt of cloth.
5 sacks of grain per bolt of cloth.
6 sacks of grain per bolt of cloth.
explanation: A price strictly between 2 and 5 rewards the cloth exporter above its cost while letting the importer buy below its own production cost. At 5 the importer has no strict gain on this margin.

title: The wage a bicycle exporter can pay
prompt: Under perfect competition, Cedar requires 3 labor hours per bicycle and 2 per basket. World prices are $18 per bicycle and $8 per basket, and both can be traded freely. Labor is mobile within Cedar. Which specialization and hourly wage are consistent with positive production?
correct: Bicycles only, with a $6 wage.
wrong: Baskets only, with a $4 wage.
Both goods, with a $5 wage.
Bicycles only, with an $18 wage.
explanation: Bicycles support 18/3=$6 per hour; baskets support only 8/2=$4. At the common $6 wage baskets cannot cover costs.

title: Consumption beyond local production
prompt: An island has 120 labor hours. A fish requires 2 hours and a jar of honey 4 hours. At a world price of one fish per jar, the island produces only fish and imports honey. After exporting 20 fish, what bundle can it consume?
correct: 40 fish and 20 jars of honey.
wrong: 20 fish and 40 jars of honey.
40 fish and 10 jars of honey.
60 fish and 20 jars of honey.
explanation: Production is 60 fish. Exporting 20 purchases 20 honey, leaving 40 fish. Producing this bundle at home would require 160 hours.

title: Productivity changes in both industries
prompt: Home initially needs 4 hours per shirt and 8 per cabinet. An innovation halves both requirements; foreign technologies are unchanged. What happens to Home's opportunity cost of a shirt?
correct: It remains one-half cabinet.
wrong: It falls from one-half to one-quarter cabinet.
It rises from one-half to one cabinet.
It falls to zero because both sectors improve.
explanation: The ratio of unit labor requirements stays 2/4=4/8. Absolute productivity rises without changing the technological opportunity cost.

title: Shipping a perishable export
prompt: A Home worker makes 6 crates per hour, while a Foreign worker makes 3. Home wages are $12 per hour; Foreign wages are $9. Half of crates shipped from Home arrive usable. Ignoring other costs, which source supplies Foreign more cheaply?
correct: Foreign production, at $3 per usable crate versus $4 for imports.
wrong: Home production, at $2 per usable crate versus $3 locally.
Home production, at $1 per usable crate versus $3 locally.
Both sources, at $3 per usable crate.
explanation: Home factory cost is $2, but two crates must be shipped per usable arrival, making delivered cost $4. Foreign cost is 9/3=$3.

title: Relative demand at a specialization boundary
prompt: In a two-country Ricardian model Home's opportunity cost of cloth is 2 food units and Foreign's is 4. At a world cloth price of 2 food units, which production pattern is consistent with competitive firms?
correct: Home can produce both goods; Foreign produces food.
wrong: Home produces only food; Foreign produces only cloth.
Both countries must produce only cloth.
Foreign can produce both goods; Home produces only cloth.
explanation: Home is indifferent between its sectors at its unit-cost ratio. Foreign finds cloth too cheap to produce and specializes in food.

title: A better export price
prompt: A small exporter sells 50 machines and spends the proceeds on imported wheat. Machine prices rise from 8 to 10 wheat units each. Holding the export quantity fixed, how much additional wheat can it purchase?
correct: 100 units.
wrong: 10 units.
50 units.
500 units.
explanation: Export purchasing power rises from 50 times 8=400 to 50 times 10=500 wheat units, a gain of 100.

title: Low wages and international competition
prompt: Home needs 1 hour per toy and Foreign needs 4. Wages are $15 in Home and $5 in Foreign. There are no trade costs. What does the unit-cost comparison imply?
correct: Home toys cost $15 versus $20 in Foreign, despite Home's higher wage.
wrong: Foreign toys cost $5 versus $15 in Home because only wages matter.
Both have the same cost because Foreign wages offset productivity exactly.
Home toys cost $60 versus $5 in Foreign after adjusting for productivity.
explanation: Unit labor cost multiplies the hourly wage by hours per unit. Low wages alone do not establish cost advantage.

title: Trade without compensation
prompt: In a frictionless one-factor Ricardian model with identical workers, free trade expands aggregate consumption possibilities. A policymaker applies this result to an economy with displaced workers and relocation costs. What is the sound interpretation?
correct: The model establishes gains under its assumptions but does not measure those workers' adjustment losses.
wrong: Expanded aggregate possibilities imply every displaced worker is immediately better off.
Relocation costs reverse comparative advantage in every industry.
Any displaced worker proves the Ricardian production calculation is incorrect.
explanation: The one-factor benchmark abstracts from heterogeneous workers and costly adjustment. Its aggregate possibility result does not quantify outcomes in a richer environment.

title: A higher price for manufacturing
prompt: In the specific-factors model, labor moves between manufacturing and agriculture; capital is fixed in manufacturing and land in agriculture. Manufacturing's price rises while agriculture's is unchanged. With diminishing marginal products and both sectors active, what happens?
correct: Labor moves to manufacturing and the wage rises by a smaller percentage than the manufacturing price.
wrong: Labor moves to agriculture and the wage falls.
Labor stays fixed because manufacturing capital is immobile.
The wage rises by a larger percentage than the manufacturing price and labor leaves manufacturing.
explanation: The higher manufacturing value marginal product attracts labor. Its marginal product then falls, so the percentage wage increase is smaller than the percentage manufacturing-price increase.

title: Workers buy both goods
prompt: In a specific-factors equilibrium, the manufacturing price rises 10%, the food price is unchanged, and the common wage rises 4%. What can be concluded about labor's real wage?
correct: It rises in food units and falls in manufactured-good units.
wrong: It rises by 4% in units of both goods.
It falls in food units and rises in manufactured-good units.
It falls by 6% in units of both goods.
explanation: The food real wage rises 4%; the manufacturing real wage changes by 1.04/1.10-1, about -5.45%. Overall worker welfare depends on consumption preferences.

title: The owner of farmland
prompt: In the standard two-sector specific-factors model, manufacturing's relative price increases and labor leaves agriculture. Food's price is fixed. What happens to the return to agriculture-specific land?
correct: It falls in units of both food and manufactures.
wrong: It rises in food units but falls in manufactures.
It stays fixed in food units because food's price is fixed.
It rises in both goods because labor becomes scarcer.
explanation: Less agricultural labor lowers the marginal product of land. Its nominal return falls while food stays fixed and manufactures become dearer.

title: A short-run factory windfall
prompt: With the other good’s price fixed, a textile price increase draws additional workers into textiles in the specific-factors model. Textile capital is fixed and complements labor. What happens to textile capital owners' purchasing power?
correct: It rises in units of textiles and of the other good.
wrong: It rises only in the other good because the textile price absorbs the whole gain.
It falls in textiles because wages rise.
It stays fixed because the capital stock cannot change.
explanation: Extra labor raises capital's marginal product. The real return in textile units rises, and the higher textile relative price reinforces the gain in the other good.

title: Calculating the labor allocation
prompt: Two sectors share 100 workers. Their value marginal products are 100-L_A and 80-L_B dollars, where L_A+L_B=100. Workers move freely and both sectors operate. What is the equilibrium allocation?
correct: 60 workers in A and 40 in B.
wrong: 50 workers in each sector.
40 workers in A and 60 in B.
80 workers in A and 20 in B.
explanation: Equalizing 100-L_A=80-(100-L_A) gives 120=2L_A, so L_A=60 and the wage is $40.

title: Immigration with fixed sector assets
prompt: A small economy has two active specific-factors sectors, fixed goods prices, diminishing labor marginal products, and complementarity between labor and each sector’s specific asset. An inflow raises total labor while sector-specific assets remain fixed. What happens to the common wage and specific-asset returns?
correct: The wage falls and returns to both specific assets rise.
wrong: The wage rises and both asset returns fall.
The wage falls and both asset returns fall.
The wage is unchanged and only the larger sector gains workers.
explanation: Additional labor lowers its marginal product in each sector and raises the marginal products of complementary specific assets. Fixed goods prices translate these into real-return changes.

title: Prices rise together
prompt: Both goods prices increase by 8% in a specific-factors economy. Technologies, endowments, and relative prices are unchanged. What is the equilibrium real effect?
correct: Labor allocation and real factor returns are unchanged.
wrong: Labor shifts to the sector with the higher initial price.
Real wages rise by 8% while real asset returns stay fixed.
Labor leaves both sectors because nominal wages lag necessarily.
explanation: A proportional increase in all goods prices scales value marginal products and nominal factor payments by the same proportion. Relative incentives and real returns stay unchanged.

title: A retraining subsidy and a model boundary
prompt: A government offers retraining to workers moving from import-competing steel to exporting services. Which assumption of the elementary specific-factors model most directly limits its ability to evaluate the program?
correct: Labor is freely mobile between sectors without retraining costs.
wrong: Capital and land are freely mobile between sectors.
Goods cannot be traded internationally.
Both sectors have constant marginal products of labor.
explanation: The elementary model treats labor as the mobile factor. Evaluating retraining requires adding mobility costs or skill differences.

title: Wage arithmetic and welfare
prompt: A worker spends a fixed half of expenditure on each of two goods with Cobb-Douglas preferences. One price rises 21%, the other stays fixed, and the wage rises 10%. There is no other income. What happens to real income measured with the exact cost-of-living index?
correct: It is unchanged.
wrong: It rises 10%.
It falls 11%.
It falls 5.5%.
explanation: The cost-of-living index rises by the square root of 1.21, or 10%. Wage and expenditure required for a given utility scale equally.

title: The horizon changes
prompt: Machines are initially usable only in textiles, but over several years can be converted to electronics. Why might the specific-factors model's prediction for textile owners become less appropriate over time?
correct: Conversion changes capital from a sector-specific factor toward a mobile factor.
wrong: Conversion prevents goods prices from affecting any factor return.
Longer horizons make comparative advantage depend only on consumer tastes.
Mobile capital must earn its old textile return after conversion costs vanish.
explanation: Factor specificity is a horizon-dependent assumption. Greater mobility changes the relevant equilibrium and distributional channels.

title: Which country is capital abundant?
prompt: North has 300 capital units and 100 workers; South has 500 capital units and 250 workers. Which country is relatively capital abundant?
correct: North, because its capital-labor ratio is 3 rather than 2.
wrong: South, because it has 500 rather than 300 capital units.
South, because it has more workers per country.
Neither, because both have more capital units than workers.
explanation: Abundance compares relative endowments, not absolute stocks. North has K/L=3 and South K/L=2.

title: The export prediction
prompt: Two countries share technologies and homothetic preferences. North is relatively capital abundant; machinery is capital intensive at all relevant factor prices. Under the standard two-good Heckscher-Ohlin assumptions, what is the predicted trade pattern?
correct: North exports machinery and imports the labor-intensive good.
wrong: North imports machinery because capital is expensive there in autarky.
North exports both goods because it has a high capital-labor ratio.
North imports the labor-intensive good only if it has fewer workers in absolute terms.
explanation: Relative capital abundance lowers the autarky relative cost of capital-intensive output and supports its export under the theorem's assumptions.

title: Price changes and real returns
prompt: In a diversified two-good Heckscher-Ohlin economy with no factor-intensity reversals, the relative price of the labor-intensive good rises. What does Stolper-Samuelson imply?
correct: Labor's real return rises in both goods; capital's falls in both.
wrong: Both real returns rise because export revenue increases.
Labor gains only in units of the capital-intensive good.
Capital gains because firms substitute capital for more expensive labor.
explanation: Under the theorem's assumptions the price increase raises the intensive factor's return more than proportionately and lowers the other factor's return.

title: More capital at fixed prices
prompt: A small, diversified economy produces a capital-intensive machine and a labor-intensive garment. At fixed goods prices, its capital endowment rises and labor stays fixed. Under standard Rybczynski assumptions, what happens to outputs?
correct: Machine output rises and garment output falls.
wrong: Both outputs rise in the same proportion.
Machine output rises and garment output stays fixed.
Garment output rises because more capital releases labor into it.
explanation: At unchanged factor prices and input coefficients, expanding the capital-intensive industry absorbs capital and draws labor from garments, which contract.

title: Recovering factor prices
prompt: At the relevant input coefficients a shirt costs 2w+r and a machine costs w+3r. Competitive prices are $10 and $15, respectively, with both goods produced. What are the wage w and rental r?
correct: w=$3 and r=$4.
wrong: w=$4 and r=$3.
w=$5 and r=$5.
w=$2 and r=$6.
explanation: The zero-profit equations 2w+r=10 and w+3r=15 imply r=4 and w=3.

title: An endowment outside diversification
prompt: Two countries have identical technologies and face the same goods prices, but one specializes completely because its endowment ratio lies outside the diversification cone. Which conclusion is warranted?
correct: Equal goods prices alone no longer guarantee equal factor prices.
wrong: Factor prices must still be equal because shipping is free.
The specialized country must have the higher wage and rental.
Specialization proves the countries have different technologies.
explanation: The usual factor-price equalization argument uses the same two active zero-profit equations in both countries. Specialization removes one of those equalities.

title: Changing intensity with factor prices
prompt: At one wage-rental ratio, food uses more capital per worker than cloth; at another, cloth uses more capital per worker than food. What standard assumption fails?
correct: The absence of factor-intensity reversals.
wrong: Identical homothetic preferences.
Constant returns to scale necessarily.
International immobility of factors necessarily.
explanation: The relative intensity ranking switches with factor prices. A fixed ranking is needed for the familiar unambiguous two-factor predictions.

title: Counting factor content
prompt: A country exports 10 machines that each embody 4 capital units and 1 labor unit. It imports 20 garments that each embody 1 capital unit and 2 labor units. Using these stated coefficients, what is its net factor content of trade?
correct: Exports 20 capital units and imports 30 labor units.
wrong: Exports 40 capital units and imports 40 labor units.
Imports 20 capital units and exports 30 labor units.
Exports 30 capital units and imports 20 labor units.
explanation: Net capital is 10(4)-20(1)=20; net labor is 10(1)-20(2)=-30. Netting imports against exports is essential.

title: Education changes the endowment
prompt: Treat skilled and unskilled labor as the two factors. Software is skill intensive and assembly is unskilled-labor intensive. A small diversified economy converts some unskilled workers into skilled workers at unchanged goods prices. Under fixed equilibrium input coefficients, what happens?
correct: Software expands and assembly contracts.
wrong: Both sectors expand because education raises total worker count.
Assembly expands because remaining unskilled workers become scarcer.
Outputs stay fixed because goods prices are fixed.
explanation: The skilled endowment rises while the unskilled endowment falls. Both changes favor skill-intensive output and reduce unskilled-intensive output under the two-factor assumptions.

title: Testing a narrow model
prompt: An analyst finds that a capital-abundant country imports a capital-intensive product. Why is this observation alone insufficient to establish an error in the standard Heckscher-Ohlin derivation?
correct: Its empirical application also requires checking technology, demand, and factor-intensity assumptions.
wrong: Relative factor abundance is defined by the observed trade pattern.
The theorem predicts only the total dollar value of trade.
Any import can be reclassified as labor intensive without examining production.
explanation: A conditional theorem can be valid even when an economy violates its premises. Product classification and model assumptions must be measured rather than assumed.

title: Spreading a design cost
prompt: A differentiated furniture producer has total cost C(q)=600+20q. Trade allows it to raise output from 30 to 60 chairs without changing this cost function. What happens to average cost?
correct: It falls from $40 to $30.
wrong: It falls from $20 to $10.
It rises from $30 to $40.
It remains $20 because marginal cost is unchanged.
explanation: Average cost is 600/q+20. Spreading the fixed cost over more chairs lowers average cost even with constant marginal cost.

title: Similar countries exchange varieties
prompt: Two countries have identical factor endowments and technologies. Consumers value different car varieties, and each variety requires a fixed production cost. Why can trade still generate gains?
correct: A larger market can support specialization in varieties and spread fixed costs.
wrong: Identical endowments imply one country has a lower opportunity cost in every variety.
Trade removes fixed costs from firms' cost functions.
Consumers gain only if imported cars use a different factor intensity.
explanation: Product differentiation and internal scale economies provide a trade motive even without traditional comparative advantage across broad industries.

title: Exporting must cover a setup cost
prompt: A firm can earn $180,000 in export revenue with variable export costs of $140,000. Entering the foreign market requires a $50,000 fixed cost for this period; domestic operations are unaffected. Should it enter for this period?
correct: No; exporting would reduce profit by $10,000.
wrong: Yes; exporting adds $180,000 in revenue.
Yes; revenue exceeds variable costs by $40,000.
No; exporting would reduce profit by $50,000.
explanation: The incremental export profit is 180,000-140,000-50,000=-10,000. Positive operating surplus is insufficient to cover entry cost.

title: Selection into exporting
prompt: In a heterogeneous-firm industry, more productive firms have lower marginal costs and larger operating profits in each market. Exporting requires a common positive fixed cost. Holding other conditions fixed, what pattern is expected?
correct: Exporters are selected disproportionately from higher-productivity firms.
wrong: Lower-productivity firms export first because their domestic sales are smaller.
Export status is unrelated to productivity because the fixed cost is common.
All surviving domestic firms export once any firm does.
explanation: The fixed export cost is easier to cover at larger operating profits. It creates a productivity cutoff above which exporting is worthwhile.

title: Reallocation without learning
prompt: Two firms have unchanged productivities of 2 and 6 units per worker. Their employment shares change from 75% and 25% to 50% and 50%. What happens to employment-weighted average productivity?
correct: It rises from 3 to 4 solely through reallocation.
wrong: It rises from 4 to 5 through within-firm improvement.
It stays at 4 because neither technology changes.
It falls from 4 to 3 because low-productivity employment shrinks.
explanation: Initially 0.75(2)+0.25(6)=3; afterward 0.5(2)+0.5(6)=4. The increase comes from weights, not firm-level learning.

title: A cluster reduces everyone's costs
prompt: A district's supplier network becomes cheaper as total industry output expands, even for individual workshops whose own output stays constant. What is this mechanism?
correct: External economies of scale at the industry level.
wrong: Internal economies from spreading each workshop's own fixed cost.
Diminishing returns to a workshop's variable input.
A movement along consumer demand caused by higher prices.
explanation: The cost reduction depends on industry scale outside the individual firm. Internal scale economies instead depend on that firm's own scale.

title: A differentiated-product markup
prompt: A monopolistically competitive firm faces a constant absolute demand elasticity of 5 and constant marginal cost $24. With an interior profit-maximizing price and no other variable costs, what price does the constant-elasticity markup rule imply?
explanation: Price equals elasticity/(elasticity-1) times marginal cost: 5/4 times 24=$30.

title: A larger market with entry
prompt: In the standard symmetric monopolistic-competition trade model, firms have fixed costs, free entry, and zero long-run economic profit. Why does an enlarged integrated market not imply permanently positive profits for incumbents?
correct: Entry and competition adjust until operating surpluses again cover fixed costs.
wrong: Fixed production costs must rise to absorb every initial gain.
Free entry forces price to equal marginal cost despite positive fixed costs.
Trade prohibits firms from earning revenue above variable cost.
explanation: Profitable opportunities attract entry. Zero total profit can coexist with a positive markup whose revenue covers fixed cost.

title: One industry, two-way trade
prompt: A country exports $80 million of pharmaceuticals and imports $60 million in the same industry. Using 1-|X-M|/(X+M), what is its intra-industry trade index?
correct: 6/7, approximately 0.857.
wrong: 1/7, approximately 0.143.
4/3, approximately 1.333.
explanation: The index is 1-20/140=120/140=6/7. It measures overlap of exports and imports, not the import-export ratio.

title: Exporters are more productive
prompt: A survey shows exporters have higher average productivity than nonexporters before their first export sale. What does this timing most directly support?
correct: Selection into exporting is a plausible explanation for part of the productivity gap.
wrong: The entire productivity gap must be caused by exporting.
Exporting cannot affect productivity after entry.
Productivity differences must reflect measurement error.
explanation: A gap that predates exporting cannot be caused solely by later export experience. It is consistent with selection, while leaving room for subsequent learning.

title: A small-country tariff
prompt: A small country can import a good at a fixed world price of $10. A specific tariff of $3 is imposed, imports remain positive, and transport is free. What domestic price results under perfect competition?
explanation: With perfectly elastic foreign supply, the tariff creates a $3 wedge above the unchanged world price.

title: Import demand after protection
prompt: Domestic demand is Q_D=100-2P and supply is Q_S=10+P. A small country faces world price 10 and introduces a tariff of 5. Imports remain positive. What are imports after the tariff?
correct: 45 units.
wrong: 60 units.
55 units.
30 units.
explanation: At P=15, demand is 70 and supply is 25, so imports are 45. Before the tariff they were 80-20=60.

title: Two distortion triangles
prompt: A small-country tariff of $4 raises domestic output by 6 units and reduces consumption by 10 units. Supply and demand are linear, the world price is fixed, and there are no other distortions. What is the national deadweight loss?
explanation: Production distortion is one-half times 4 times 6=$12; consumption distortion is one-half times 4 times 10=$20. Revenue is a transfer within the country.

title: Who receives quota rents?
prompt: A binding import quota permits 40 units. The domestic price is $15 and the world price $10, with no transport cost. The government auctions licenses competitively. What is quota-license revenue?
explanation: The rent per imported unit is the $5 price wedge. Auctioning 40 licenses captures 40 times 5=$200 for the government.

title: Licenses given abroad
prompt: A small country replaces a tariff with an import quota producing the same domestic price and quantity. Tariff revenue had been $200; under the quota foreign exporters receive all rents. Other conditions are identical. What happens to home national welfare relative to the tariff?
correct: It falls by $200.
wrong: It is unchanged because quantities are identical.
It rises by $200 because the government no longer collects tax.
It falls by the entire value of imports.
explanation: Consumer and domestic producer surpluses are unchanged, but the $200 previously collected at home now accrues abroad.

title: Demand increases under a quota
prompt: A small country has either a fixed specific tariff or an initially equivalent binding quantity quota. World supply is perfectly elastic. Domestic demand then increases. How do the policies differ?
correct: Imports can rise under the tariff; under the quota the domestic price rises to limit imports.
wrong: Imports stay fixed under the tariff but rise under the quota.
Both policies keep the domestic price and imports fixed.
The quota automatically expands to preserve the initial price wedge.
explanation: The tariff fixes the price wedge while allowing quantity to adjust. The quota fixes import quantity, so stronger demand increases scarcity rents and the domestic price.

title: A large importer's terms of trade
prompt: A tariff by a large importer reduces the foreign export price. Which comparison determines whether the tariff raises that importer's national welfare, ignoring retaliation and other distortions?
correct: The terms-of-trade gain versus domestic production and consumption distortion losses.
wrong: Tariff revenue versus the entire value of domestic consumption.
The export-price decline versus domestic producer gains alone.
The change in import quantity versus the change in export quantity alone.
explanation: Unlike a small country, a large importer may transfer surplus from foreign sellers through a lower export price. That gain must exceed its own distortion costs.

title: Protection of value added
prompt: A bicycle sells for $100 under free trade and uses an imported component costing $60. A tariff raises the bicycle price to $110, while an input tariff raises the component price to $66. Coefficients are fixed. What is the effective protection rate on domestic value added?
explanation: Free-trade value added is $40; protected value added is $44. The increase of $4 divided by $40 is 10%.

title: A subsidy with a production externality
prompt: A small open economy has a positive external benefit of domestic production but no other market distortions. The world price is fixed and policy administration is costless, and subsidies can be financed by nondistortionary lump-sum taxes. Which instrument directly targets the distortion?
correct: A production subsidy equal to the marginal external benefit at the efficient output.
wrong: An import tariff that taxes domestic consumption as well as encouraging production.
An export tax that reduces the producer price.
A consumption subsidy regardless of where the good is produced.
explanation: A production subsidy aligns the private and social production margins without distorting the consumption price. A tariff also suppresses consumption unnecessarily.

title: An export subsidy in a small country
prompt: A small exporting country pays $2 per unit exported. With competition, no transport costs, and continued exports, what happens to its domestic price relative to the fixed world price?
correct: It rises by $2 because sellers can earn the world price plus subsidy abroad.
wrong: It falls by $2 because the government pays part of production costs.
It stays equal to the world price because the country is small.
It rises only if the subsidy is paid to domestic consumers.
explanation: Arbitrage equalizes domestic sales returns with subsidized export returns. Domestic buyers must match the world price plus the subsidy.

title: A gravity-model prediction
prompt: In a simplified gravity equation, bilateral trade is proportional to exporter GDP times importer GDP divided by distance. Exporter GDP rises 20%, importer GDP rises 10%, and distance is unchanged. Holding the equation's other terms fixed, what is the predicted trade increase?
explanation: The new product is 1.20 times 1.10=1.32 of the old one. Percentage changes compound.

title: Distance in logarithms
prompt: A hypothetical regression of log trade on log distance has slope -1.2 on log distance. For a 10% increase in distance, by what exact factor does the exponentiated fitted value change, holding all other regressors fixed?
correct: 1.10 raised to -1.2, approximately 0.892.
wrong: 1.10 raised to 1.2, approximately 1.121.
1.20 raised to -1.1, approximately 0.818.
explanation: Exponentiating the fitted log change gives 1.10 raised to -1.2. The exact decrease is about 10.8%; 12% is a local approximation. This concerns the exponentiated fit, not a claim about the conditional arithmetic mean without retransformation assumptions.

title: A missing zero-trade pair
prompt: An analyst estimates log trade on observed positive flows and drops country pairs with zero trade. What issue should be investigated before generalizing the results?
correct: The selected positive-flow sample may differ systematically from pairs with zero trade.
wrong: A zero trade flow necessarily means the distance measure is zero.
Dropping zero flows makes every slope estimate equal to zero.
Taking logs of positive values mechanically removes all heteroskedasticity.
explanation: The extensive margin may be related to trade costs and other regressors. Excluding zeros changes the sample and may affect interpretation.

title: Relative remoteness
prompt: Two equally large markets are equally distant from a seller. Market A is near many alternative suppliers; market B is remote from them. Why can their imports from this seller differ even with identical bilateral distance?
correct: Trade depends on costs relative to alternative trading opportunities as well as bilateral costs.
wrong: Gravity implies distance matters only when GDP differs.
Remoteness must eliminate all imports into market B.
The seller's production technology must differ by destination.
explanation: Alternative sources and markets affect relative trade resistance. Bilateral distance and size alone do not exhaust the relevant opportunities.

title: Imported inputs and gross exports
prompt: A firm exports a product for $200. It uses $120 of imported inputs and creates the remaining value domestically; assume no other foreign content or double counting within the firm. What domestic value added is embodied in the export?
explanation: Gross exports include foreign input value. Subtracting imported content leaves $200-$120=$80 of domestic value added.
skill: distinguish gross trade from value added

title: The offshoring break-even quantity
prompt: Performing a task at home costs $9 per unit. Offshoring costs $5 per unit plus a fixed coordination cost of $20,000, with identical quality and no other costs. At what volume do the two options have equal total cost?
correct: 5,000 units.
wrong: 4,000 units.
2,222 units, approximately.
20,000 units.
explanation: Equating 9q=5q+20,000 gives q=5,000. Above that volume the $4 unit saving outweighs the fixed cost.

title: Offshoring and the skill mix
prompt: A home firm moves its least skill-intensive stage abroad while keeping its more skill-intensive stages. Holding the input use of every remaining domestic stage fixed, what happens mechanically to the average skill intensity of its remaining domestic activity?
correct: It rises because the least skill-intensive stage is removed.
wrong: It falls because some jobs have moved abroad.
It is unchanged because no stage changes technology.
It rises only if the foreign stage is more skill intensive than all home stages.
explanation: Changing the composition of domestic tasks can raise average skill intensity without within-stage technical change. This is a composition result, not a complete wage prediction.

title: An exposed region before the shock
prompt: A study compares employment changes in regions with high and low import exposure. High-exposure regions were already declining faster before the import increase. What is the principal concern for a simple difference-in-differences interpretation?
correct: The untreated parallel-trends assumption is less credible.
wrong: Treatment effects must be positive because employment initially differed.
Any difference in initial employment levels alone invalidates difference-in-differences.
Preexisting trends guarantee that the estimated effect is exactly zero.
explanation: Different prior trends raise concern that post-period differences partly reflect continuing nontrade forces. Equal initial levels are not the identifying requirement.

title: Trade agreements and causality
prompt: A regression associates trade-agreement membership with greater bilateral trade. Countries may sign agreements when trade is already expected to grow. Why is the membership coefficient not automatically a causal effect?
correct: Agreement formation may be correlated with unobserved determinants of future trade.
wrong: An agreement indicator cannot be included in a regression with GDP.
Reverse causality implies agreements must reduce trade.
A positive coefficient proves all trade costs have vanished.
explanation: Anticipated trade growth can influence agreement formation, creating selection or omitted-variable bias. A causal interpretation needs an identification strategy.

title: A local loss and an aggregate gain
prompt: Suppose a credible study finds persistent earnings losses among workers in regions exposed to import competition, while a separate model predicts a positive national consumption gain. Which statement best reconciles these results?
correct: Aggregate gains can coexist with concentrated losses when gains are unevenly distributed and compensation is incomplete.
wrong: The national gain logically implies exposed workers' earnings cannot fall.
The local losses establish that national real consumption must fall by the same amount.
Compensation is automatic whenever cheaper imports raise consumer surplus.
explanation: National welfare and local labor-market outcomes measure different objects. Consumer gains and other gains need not reach displaced workers or offset their individual losses.
